intro: Sentence-final な has two separate jobs. Drawn out as なあ after a plain sentence, it lets a feeling escape, with no need for anyone to reply: いいなあ, 'how nice'. Short and sharp after a verb's dictionary form, it is a blunt ban: 行くな, 'don't go'. What it attaches to, and how long it is, tell the two apart.

skills.rule: End a plain-form sentence with なあ (or short な) to voice a feeling or thought to yourself: 'how ...!', 'I'd really love to ...'.
skills.explain:
なあ lets an emotion out: admiration (きれいだなあ), envy (いいなあ), longing (海に行きたいなあ), mild complaint (疲れたなあ, 遅いなあ). Nobody has to be there to hear it; it is what you mutter at a sunset or on a stalled train. With a listener present it still reports your own feeling rather than asking for theirs.

It follows plain forms. Verbs and い-adjectives attach directly (寒いなあ, 降ってきたなあ); nouns and な-adjectives take だ first (静かだなあ, 雨だなあ). After です or ます it sounds like an elderly man (いいですなあ); in polite speech say ですね instead.

Short な in casual, mostly male speech also works as a soft ね towards the listener: そうだな, 'yeah, let me think'; 明日来るよな, 'you're coming tomorrow, right?'. The edge with ね: ね reaches out for agreement, なあ stays inside your head.

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]い{なあ}。
海[うみ]がきれいだ{なあ}。
田中[たなか]さんはよく食[た]べる{なあ}。
夏休[なつやす]みが待[ま]ち遠[どお]しい{なあ}。
examples.en: I can't wait for the summer holidays.

examples.jp: 一度[いちど]でいいから、富士山[ふじさん]に登[のぼ]りたい{なあ}。
examples.en: Just once, I'd love to climb Mount Fuji.

contrast.note: ね is addressed to someone and invites them to share the feeling: 寒いですね to a colleague. 寒いなあ is what you say to yourself, alone at the bus stop.
よ tells a listener something new: 外は寒いよ, 'it's cold out, you know (take a coat)'. なあ informs no one; it only reacts.
かな wonders about something you do not know: 雨かな, 'I wonder if it'll rain'. なあ reacts to something you see or feel: 雨だなあ, 'rain again, ugh'.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]、今日[きょう]は暑[あつ]いです{なあ}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]、今日[きょう]は暑[あつ]いです{ね}。
mistakes.note: ですなあ sounds like an old man holding forth. To a teacher, share the feeling with ですね.

mistakes.bad: この公園[こうえん]は静[しず]か{なあ}。
mistakes.good: この公園[こうえん]は静[しず]かだ{なあ}。
mistakes.note: Nouns and な-adjectives need だ before なあ.

skills.tip: Could you say it to nobody, with a sigh? Then なあ.

skills.rule: Verb dictionary form + な means 'don't!': a blunt, direct ban (行くな, 'don't go').
skills.explain:
Attach な to the dictionary form of a verb, always the affirmative form: 走るな, 'don't run'; 忘れるな, 'don't forget'; 心配するな, 'don't worry'. It is the plain negative command, the mirror of the imperative (走れ, 'run!'). You hear it from coaches, from parents shouting, between close male friends, in fiction, and on blunt signs (触るな, 押すな).

It is rude to anyone you should be polite to. The everyday request is ないで or ないでください: 走らないでください, 'please don't run'. Use するな only when the English is a curt order.

Do not confuse it with masu-stem + な (行きな, 食べな), a casual, kindly command meaning the opposite: 'go on, go', 'eat up'. 食べるな is 'don't eat'; 食べな is 'eat'. Length matters too: the ban is short and falling, while a drawn-out よく食べるなあ is musing, 'you sure eat a lot'.

examples.jp: 心配[しんぱい]する{な}。大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だ。
ここに車[くるま]を止[と]める{な}。
最後[さいご]まであきらめる{な}！
examples.en: Don't give up until the very end!

examples.jp: 二度[にど]とうそをつく{な}。

contrast.note: ないでください is the polite request: 走らないでください, 'please don't run'. 走るな is a command with no softening at all.
行きな and 食べな tell someone to DO the action, casually and kindly ('go on, go'). After the dictionary form, な forbids it.
A long, musing なあ after a dictionary form comments on what someone does: よく寝るなあ, 'you sure sleep a lot'. The ban is a short, sharp な.

mistakes.note: Prohibitive な takes the dictionary form, never the ます form.

mistakes.good: （'Don't eat it!'）それを食[た]べる{な}！
mistakes.note: 食べな means 'eat it'. The ban needs the full dictionary form 食べる.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]、心配[しんぱい]する{な}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]、心配[しんぱい]しないでください。
mistakes.note: A blunt order to a teacher is rude. Use the polite request ないでください.

skills.tip: Dictionary form + short な is a stop sign. Drawn out (なあ) or after the stem (食べな), it is not a ban.
